claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy has a uniform, self-forming passive oxide film that protects it under static, benign conditions.
Overall tribo-corrosion degradation is governed by cyclic removal and reformation of the passive oxide film.
Controlled sliding wear intermittently removes the native passive oxide film.
Removal of the passive film exposes the underlying metal.
The newly exposed metal undergoes accelerated corrosion.
Corrosion-resistant elements in the alloy drive rapid repassivation of exposed areas.
Repassivation partially restores the protective oxide film between wear events.
Continuous film removal and reformation couples the wear and corrosion processes.
Wear-induced material loss under tribo-corrosion will exceed that under matched wear-only conditions.
Corrosion depth under tribo-corrosion will be lower than under static corrosion-only conditions because of partial repassivation.
Total degradation under tribo-corrosion will not equal the simple sum of independent wear-only and corrosion-only degradation.
The proposed mechanism should operate when repassivation is sufficiently rapid under moderate wear.
Extremely high mechanical loads can overwhelm repassivation and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Highly aggressive electrolytes can prevent oxide reformation and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
The balance between mechanical damage and repassivation depends on the alloy system and test parameters.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says sliding removes protection and accelerates corrosion, while the corrosion-only baseline permits undisturbed oxide formation; nevertheless, the prediction assigns lower corrosion depth to the mechanically disrupted tribo-corrosion condition. Partial repassivation alone does not explain why protection would surpass the undisturbed static baseline.

The hypothesis states that sliding mechanically removes the passive film, whereas the wear-only baseline is described as using an inert electrolyte that preserves the passive film despite applying the same sliding. An inert electrolyte can suppress corrosion but cannot by itself ensure preservation against mechanical removal.
